justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near current market levels and gradually climbing from roughly 107.5 at one day out to 109.5 at one month. The one-day estimate is anchored primarily by recent price momentum and the assumption that no major overnight catalysts materialize, so it sits close to whatever the prevailing level was at forecast time. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher on the assumption that the underlying trend, whether in an equity index, commodity, or currency pair, carries mild positive momentum without a significant reversal. The one-month estimate extends that logic further, incorporating a baseline expectation that macroeconomic conditions remain broadly supportive and that any mean-reversion forces are modest relative to trend continuation.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.4 units, capturing normal intraday and overnight volatility, scheduled data releases, and the possibility of modest surprise in either direction. At one week, the interval nearly doubles to about 11 units, because a full week introduces earnings announcements, central bank commentary, geopolitical headlines, and the simple accumulation of daily random variation. At one month, the interval expands to 25 units, acknowledging that a full calendar month is long enough for regime shifts in sentiment, significant policy changes, or sector-level rotations to materially alter the price path. Historical realized volatility at each horizon informed these widths.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals entirely. On the upside, an unexpected policy pivot — such as a surprise rate cut, a major fiscal stimulus announcement, or a geopolitical resolution that markets had priced pessimistically — could drive prices well above the upper bound of any horizon. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in credit conditions, an unanticipated inflation print, or a geopolitical escalation could break through the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is more time for negative feedback loops to develop. Liquidity events, such as a large forced seller or a flash-crash dynamic, could temporarily breach even the one-day interval, though such moves would likely partially reverse.

It is also worth noting that the intervals assume a roughly log-normal distribution of returns with stationary volatility, which is itself a simplification. In practice, volatility clusters and can spike abruptly, meaning the tails are fatter than a normal approximation implies. If implied volatility were to reprice sharply — as it does during market stress — the true uncertainty at each horizon would be considerably wider than what I have stated.
